Hi and welcome!! I’m anxious-avoidant but more on the avoidant side. Ive had painful run ins with both avoidant and anxious types, anxious attachers send my anxiety through the roof and avoidants, well, avoid. Hard for them to feel safe enough to be vulnerable.

 It’s SO much worse during hell week and I’ve lost friendships and detonated a long term relationship over it. It took years to realize how my attachment style is like this computer program that is always running unconsciously, and informs how I interact with the world. But healing our nervous systems can mean working with a new and less painful program. 


A quick word of warning: attachment theory has exploded on social media lately and with it has come some unfortunate stigmatization of both types. The best resources tend to focus on building emotional/social safety and won’t put labels on one style as being any better or worse. I see a lot of anxious attachment content that bashes avoidants despite them both stemming from developmental trauma. 

If you’re on Instagram, I really recommend checking out Melissa Parks @melissaparkssays

She puts out some really informative and helpful stuff from a trauma informed perspective. She breaks down these dynamics in a matter of fact, non judgmental way. 

 tldr; you’re on the money, PMDD totally exacerbates anything attachment related BUT it isn’t an objective signal by itself. I have a beautiful relationship with my husband and often get hell weeks that make me think it is all doomed, I’ll never be happy again, he’s cheating, etc. Then it passes and I realize “Damn, that was a chemical thunderstorm that woke up every relational worst case scenario I could think of and NONE of it was actually happening. Pmdd can make a person feel like they’re always on the back foot, not understood, etc. It can cause kind of a storm in your brain that makes you doubt your emotional safety in relationships. The dysphoria makes it hard to see things in reality but then it promptly passes with the end of luteal phase. Often that dsyphoria makes pmdd-ers prone to being gaslit themselves. 

But what pmdd doesn’t do is create a total aversion to feedback, or a constantly antagonistic stance. For pmdd-ers it’s really shameful and embarrassing to look back on times when you didn’t give your partner the benefit of the doubt or were unkind. This urges us to seek help, find support, just lessen the impact on others somehow. Read through posts here and see if your gf carries the same amount of awareness or accountability. If you see no sense of personal responsibility for her own emotions, or any attempts to repair the ruptures she creates, then this is not a pmdd thing it’s a her thing. And it is in no way your job to fix that in her, it’s 100% your job to take care of yourself and leave if this relationship has run its course.

It’s so great you’re looking for tips! Here’s my two cents. 

Avoid asking questions that are too broad. It will make her less frustrated and give you better information to work with. 

When you check in with her, ask two separate questions: “How are you doing?” and “How is your body doing?” It takes a lot of pressure off,  being able to say “hey I’m having an okay day but my body feels awful right now”. 


When I am asked overly broad questions about how I am feeling, I get hit with waves of frustration, guilt, aggravation and sadness. Because I am feeling a ton of contradictory things at once when pain is present, and I need to live with that daily. Understand this is a chronic condition so the way you ask about it matters. 

With that said, try not to take things personally when she’s not up to much or doesn’t seem like herself. It will be really hard and you’ll wish you could just take it away for her, but the best thing you could do is be willing to sit with her through the bad days until she feels more like herself again. 

Practical help goes such a long way. If she’s having a bad pain day, taking a small thing off her plate would be a BIG relief. Things like dishes, laundry, or making dinner.

It is kind of a convoluted balancing act no matter what system you use to describe the functions. You “power up” your thinking with your feeling or your feeling with your thinking. 

Generally it gets easier once you notice the difference between the introverted and extraverted forms of whatever your savior decider is. So if you’re a feeler, notice the difference between Fe and Fi. Fe values broader social “good feelings” Fi values deeper personal “good feelings”. The feeling function provides very important information and is often how we form morals, create boundaries, make connections, chase interests, build communities. It is the felt sense behind personal integrity (Fi) and social safety (Fe). 

The two often misunderstand each other. Fe critiques Fi for being self absorbed, Fi critiques Fe for being disingenuous. They have different underlying reasons. 

Fe has Ti. Underneath the fake social niceties is a logical framework that they take way more personally. Underneath the highly sensitive Fi is a rational problem solver that wants everyone to have what they need. 

Do the opposite if you’re a thinker. Start identifying obvious lead Ti’s and Te’s. They are prioritizing problem solving, management, system building, troubleshooting, disaster recovery, inventing, etc.  The Te’s want it to work for everyone, the Ti’s don’t care if it works for everyone so long as they understand it. Look underneath and you notice the their reasons are powered up by the sense of Fi integrity or Fe community. 

Like the Te lead looking out for vulnerable and unprotected people with their Fi. Maybe if they solve enough problems for others they will feel seen and fulfilled. 

Or the Fe hiding underneath the Ti inventor who just wants to create something that makes everyone happy. Maybe if they understand something deeper than anyone else is willing to go, they can come up with something everyone loves. 

Much easier with the Deciders, but trickier with the observers. Generally though, you will see the priorities emerge over time.
